title: Piston Brings Cardless Fleet Fuel Payments to 341 Jacksons Stores
snippet: The cardless fleet payment network is now live at all Jacksons Food Stores locations across eight western US states, expanding its merchant footprint. The post Piston Brings Cardless Fleet Fuel Payments to 341 Jacksons Stores appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Piston, a Cupertino-based cardless payment network serving commercial fleets, has gone live at 341 Jacksons Food Stores locations across eight western US states. The rollout represents one of the larger single-partner expansions in the company’s history and takes Piston’s total merchant coverage to more than 3,000 fuel stations across 48 states.

The partnership gives fleet operators on Piston’s network additional fuelling options when planning routes in the western US, while Jacksons gains a channel to attract commercial fuel volume without adding a new card scheme or open-loop network. Piston replaces the physical fleet card with mobile authorisation tied to a specific driver and vehicle, giving fleet managers real-time spend visibility at the transaction level.

How the network model works

Piston’s commercial proposition rests on a direct integration at the point of sale rather than routing through the traditional card-network stack. The company says this removes four intermediaries from the standard transaction chain, improving the economics for both the fuel retailer and the fleet. Direct POS integration also gives Piston access to richer transaction data than an open-loop card network would see, which the company says underpins its fraud-prevention tooling.

That fraud layer now includes Piston Guard, a real-time tool that can flag or block suspected fraudulent purchases before settlement, and Piston Analytics Agent, which surfaces spending patterns for fleet operators. Both are positioned as AI-assisted capabilities, though the release did not provide performance benchmarks or third-party validation for either product.

Cory Jackson, president of Jacksons Food Stores, said that commercial fuelling is a meaningful part of the chain’s business and that the way fleets pay is shifting. “Working with Piston helps us keep pace with that shift and makes Jacksons a practical stop for fleets using modern payment technology,” he said.

Market context and competitive positioning

The US fleet card market is a well-established segment dominated by WEX, Fleetcor and Comdata, all of which operate large closed-loop or open-loop networks with deep integrations into fuel retailers and telematics providers. Piston’s bet is that a cardless, mobile-first network built on direct POS partnerships can undercut incumbents on cost and out-compete them on data granularity and fraud prevention.

The growth figures cited in the release are notable if accurate. Piston reported an eightfold increase in payment volume and a fortyfold expansion of its merchant network over the past year, though no base figures were provided, making the absolute scale difficult to assess. The company also noted that its POS integrations are certified on systems representing more than 95 percent of US merchant fuel sites, a figure that, if independently verified, would represent significant infrastructure coverage for a business of this age.

Piston closed a $15 million Series A round led by FPV Ventures earlier this year, with participation from existing backers Spark Capital and Pear VC, taking total funding to $22.5 million. The company said it intends to use that capital to onboard additional fuel retailers, expand product capabilities and grow headcount. At $22.5 million in total funding, Piston remains lightly capitalised relative to its stated ambitions. The pace of merchant network growth will be the clearest indicator of whether the direct-partnership model can scale before better-resourced incumbents respond.

title: PayPal Urges Retailers to Show BNPL Earlier as Black Friday Nears
snippet: PayPal research finds 67% of Christmas BNPL shoppers are more likely to add items to their basket when payment options appear on product pages. The post PayPal Urges Retailers to Show BNPL Earlier as Black Friday Nears appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
PayPal has published research ahead of the Black Friday and Cyber Monday peak, warning UK retailers that late disclosure of buy now, pay later options is costing them basket additions. The payments group says nine in ten UK adults are actively managing festive spending, and that visibility of instalment-payment options earlier in the shopping journey can materially shift conversion.

The research, conducted by Morning Consult on behalf of PayPal between 4 and 10 September 2026 among 2,076 UK adults, found that more than half of Christmas BNPL shoppers (55%) would favour a retailer that shows the option on product pages over one that waits until the checkout step, where only 21% said they preferred to see it. Two-thirds (67%) said earlier visibility would make them more likely to add an item to their basket. PayPal also cited its own internal data showing an 11% uplift in PayPal payment volumes among merchants that introduced Pay Later messaging or a second checkout button, though it noted results may vary and the underlying merchant sample dated from March 2020 to September 2025.

The BNPL placement argument

The distinction between product-page and checkout-page disclosure is commercially significant. At checkout, a shopper has already decided in principle to buy; instalment framing at that point reduces friction but does not drive discovery. On the product page, showing a weekly or monthly cost alongside a headline price addresses affordability earlier, when the shopper is still deciding whether to proceed. For higher-consideration purchases, that reframing can be the deciding factor.

UK home fitness retailer JTX Fitness offered a case study in the release. Jamie Forshaw, head of marketing at JTX Fitness, said: “Showing customers their payment options while they’re still browsing can help them feel more confident about how they’ll manage the cost. When customers can see Pay Later from the product page onwards, more of them go from browsing to buying.”

Sean Douglas, senior director of UK Large Enterprise at PayPal, noted that peak season pressure tends to put retailers in survival mode, but argued the data pointed to a more active opportunity: the 11% volume uplift, he said, could be the difference between meeting revenue targets and exceeding them.

Market context and regulatory backdrop

PayPal’s Pay Later sits within a BNPL market that is under active regulatory review in the UK. The Financial Conduct Authority has been developing a framework to bring point-of-sale credit products within the Consumer Credit Act perimeter, a process that has run for several years and is expected to introduce affordability check requirements, clearer pre-contract disclosure rules and new marketing standards. Once the regime is live, the question of where and how BNPL options are surfaced to consumers will move from a commercial optimisation decision to a compliance one.

The broader market for embedded BNPL includes Klarna, Clearpay (Afterpay) and Zilch, each of which also promotes early product-page integration to merchant partners. PayPal’s advantage in this space is distribution: its existing merchant acceptance network and buyer-side login reduce integration friction compared with a standalone BNPL provider. The research release is also a vehicle for directing merchants to PayPal’s Pay Later onboarding page, so the findings should be read in that commercial context.

The AI finding is a secondary data point worth watching. More than a third of respondents (35%) said they had used or planned to use AI for Christmas shopping, and 52% said they would use it specifically to find deals or compare prices. If AI-assisted browsing compresses the product discovery phase, the window in which payment messaging can influence a shopper may shift again, adding further complexity to where in the journey BNPL should appear.

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Visa and Mesh Partner to Bring Crypto Balances to 175m Merchants
snippet: The partnership lets consumers pay directly from crypto or stablecoin wallets at any Visa-accepting merchant, with no card pre-load required. The post Visa and Mesh Partner to Bring Crypto Balances to 175m Merchants appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Visa and Mesh have announced a strategic partnership designed to make crypto and stablecoin balances spendable across Visa’s global acceptance network of 175 million merchant locations in more than 200 countries. The deal targets what Mesh describes as the last-mile problem in digital-asset payments: the friction between owning crypto and actually spending it.

The mechanics are straightforward in principle. Mesh provisions a Visa credential behind the scenes when a consumer wants to pay. The user taps or checks out online as normal; the merchant receives a standard card payment with no new hardware or workflow changes required. Mesh handles the funding, conversion and, where required, KYC and user onboarding, acting as programme manager. The consumer does not need to pre-sell holdings, transfer funds to a bank account, or sign up for a separate card linked to a single platform.

The last-mile problem in context

The release cites Crypto.com research putting global crypto ownership at 774 million people as of June 2026. Yet American Banker data referenced in the release puts monthly crypto card volumes at roughly $1.5 billion by late 2025, a figure that, set against Visa’s $14.2 trillion in fiscal 2025 payment volume, illustrates how little of that ownership has converted into everyday spending. The gap is not primarily a product of consumer reluctance; it reflects the structural friction of existing rails. Every current route from a stablecoin balance to a fiat point-of-sale transaction requires a prior action by the consumer.

Mesh says it already serves more than 200 enterprise clients, including Kalshi, Tools for Humanity, Félix Pago, Majority and KAST, and its network connects hundreds of wallets, exchanges and platforms. That existing distribution is the commercial logic of the Visa deal: Visa brings ubiquitous merchant acceptance, and Mesh brings the orchestration layer that aggregates fragmented digital-asset balances.

“Crypto never had a spending problem, it has a last-mile problem, and until now, closing it meant getting a separate card,” said Bam Azizi, chief executive and co-founder of Mesh. “Mesh handles the funding and conversion, so a balance becomes purchasing power at the moment of payment, with nothing for the user to move and nothing for the merchant to change.”

Competitive and regulatory read-across

The partnership sits inside a broader push by card networks to integrate digital assets into traditional payment flows. Visa has previously worked with Circle and other stablecoin issuers on settlement rails, and Mastercard has pursued similar orchestration partnerships. The differentiator Mesh is positioning here is wallet-agnosticism: rather than tying the experience to a single issuer or platform, Mesh aggregates across wallets so a consumer can spend from whichever balance they hold, wherever they happen to be.

On the regulatory side, stablecoin payment infrastructure is drawing increasing legislative attention in both the US and the EU. In the US, the Genius Act and parallel House bills are progressing through Congress and would establish a federal licensing framework for stablecoin issuers, potentially clarifying the compliance path for programme managers like Mesh. In the EU, MiCA’s asset-referenced token provisions are already live, and the European Central Bank is watching stablecoin payment volumes with close interest. Neither development blocks the Visa-Mesh model, but both will shape how quickly participating platforms can onboard users in regulated jurisdictions.

The announcement does not confirm a launch date, name the first participating wallet platforms beyond existing Mesh clients, or disclose commercial terms. Rollout details are described as forthcoming. The key near-term markers are the jurisdictions where the product goes live first, the stablecoin denominations supported at launch, and whether any major consumer wallet outside Mesh’s existing enterprise roster signs on.

title: FCA AI Review Prompts Call to Keep Customer Needs Central
snippet: EQWIRE CEO Sophie Njagi urges fintechs to anchor AI product development in customer needs, citing the FCA's latest AI good-practice findings. The post FCA AI Review Prompts Call to Keep Customer Needs Central appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The Financial Conduct Authority published its latest review of AI use in financial services this week, identifying examples of good practice alongside areas requiring improvement. The regulator highlighted the importance of defining customer needs before building products, maintaining effective human oversight of AI systems, and ensuring operational resilience. Sophie Njagi, chief executive of UK-regulated Electronic Money Institution EQWIRE, has used the findings to call on fintech businesses to place those principles at the core of product development.

Njagi’s central argument is that commercial enthusiasm for AI is creating a gap between what looks impressive in a product demonstration and what actually serves customers at scale. “Products can look impressive in a demonstration but struggle when customers start using them at scale,” she said. “The test is whether they solve a meaningful problem, make the customer’s experience simpler and have the operations behind them to deliver reliably.”

What the FCA found

The regulator’s review did not name firms but outlined a pattern: financial services businesses are deploying AI tools with insufficient clarity about the customer problem being addressed, and with oversight frameworks that have not kept pace with the capabilities being introduced. Operational resilience, a concept the FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority have embedded in formal rules for several years, featured prominently as an area where AI deployments are lagging.

The findings carry weight in a regulatory environment that is moving quickly. The FCA has signalled a pro-innovation stance on AI but has been equally clear that the Consumer Duty, which came into full force in 2023, requires firms to demonstrate good outcomes for retail customers. That creates a compliance obligation, not merely a design preference, to understand what customers need before committing engineering resource to building.

Five principles for durable product development

Njagi sets out five principles that she argues produce technology products built to last. These cover prioritising genuinely important customer problems over fashionable technology trends; investing in operational foundations rather than surface-layer design; managing complexity internally so customers experience simplicity; building teams with genuine ownership of outcomes; and maintaining the strategic flexibility to change direction as regulation, technology and customer behaviour shift.

The principles are not novel, but the FCA context gives them a compliance dimension that pure product advice lacks. For fintech founders and product leaders, the regulator’s findings amount to a signal that AI roadmaps will receive scrutiny on customer-outcome grounds, not only on technical-risk grounds.

Market context

The FCA review lands in a period of intense AI adoption across retail banking, payments and lending. Established banks and challenger firms alike are integrating large-language-model tooling into customer-facing and back-office processes. The risk the regulator appears most concerned about is the adoption of AI capabilities that are genuinely impressive in controlled conditions but whose performance, edge-case handling and failure modes are not well understood by the firms deploying them.

For smaller fintechs and EMIs operating under tighter capital and compliance resource constraints, the operational resilience requirement is particularly pointed. Building the oversight infrastructure that regulators expect around AI systems adds cost that must be justified by the customer outcome delivered. Njagi’s framing, from the perspective of a CEO running a regulated EMI, is that the discipline required by regulation and the discipline required by good product development are effectively the same thing.

title: COLIBRIX ONE Taps Vivox AI for Automated KYB Merchant Onboarding
snippet: The FCA- and MFSA-authorised payments platform will use Vivox AI's explainable agents to verify corporate documents and run sanctions screening on new merchants. The post COLIBRIX ONE Taps Vivox AI for Automated KYB Merchant Onboarding appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
COLIBRIX ONE, the payments infrastructure platform operated within the Mellifera group, has selected Vivox AI under a multi-year agreement to automate know-your-business checks across its UK and EU merchant base. The deal is designed to reduce the time compliance analysts spend processing document-heavy due diligence on new business customers without removing human sign-off from the process.

Under the arrangement, Vivox AI’s explainable AI agents will handle corporate document verification, ultimate beneficial owner mapping, and sanctions and adverse media screening. Every AI-generated finding is traceable to its underlying source, and COLIBRIX ONE’s compliance team will review and approve each case before it is closed. The rollout covers merchant onboarding in the UK and EU, with plans to extend to ongoing monitoring and additional entity types in 2027.

What the technology does

Vivox AI’s agents draw on corporate registry data across more than 155 countries to identify ownership structures, shareholders and directors, then generate a full customer due diligence or enhanced due diligence report for analyst review. In an earlier deployment at international payments firm TransferMate, the company said due diligence time fell from roughly 60 minutes to under 15 minutes per case, with screening alerts declining by 86 per cent. Those figures come from Vivox AI’s own account of the TransferMate project and have not been independently verified.

Tim Khamzin, founder and chief executive of Vivox AI, said: “AI agents take on the document-heavy due diligence work where every conclusion comes with a clear audit trail, so analysts stay in control and regulators can see exactly how a decision was reached. That is what makes AI usable in a regulated business.”

COLIBRIX ONE is authorised by the UK Financial Conduct Authority as an electronic money institution (FRN 927920) and holds a parallel authorisation through Mellifera Kartiera Limited from the Malta Financial Services Authority. Its product stack includes card acquiring for one-time and recurring transactions, multi-currency current accounts with dedicated named IBANs, and global payouts, with principal memberships at Visa and Mastercard.

Regulatory and market context

The timing reflects a specific pressure on payment platforms regulated under UK and EU financial crime frameworks. The FCA has tightened its expectations on anti-money laundering controls and merchant due diligence for e-money institutions in recent years, and the EU’s AML package, including the forthcoming AML Authority, will raise baseline obligations further across the bloc. For platforms that compete partly on onboarding speed, manual KYB on merchants with complex, multi-jurisdiction ownership structures is a genuine operational bottleneck.

The market for AI-assisted compliance tooling is expanding quickly. Established regtech vendors and a new generation of AI-native compliance firms are competing to automate the same document-heavy workflows, often positioning explainability and audit-trail quality as the differentiator that makes their products acceptable to risk functions and supervisors alike. COLIBRIX ONE’s choice of a dedicated AI compliance vendor rather than a bundled solution from its existing technology stack reflects a broader pattern among licensed payment firms: separating the compliance workflow layer from the core processing infrastructure in order to swap components as the tooling matures.

The key variable to watch in deployments like this one is whether the efficiency gains cited from the TransferMate reference hold across a larger and more varied merchant portfolio, particularly for merchants with layered holding structures in higher-risk jurisdictions, where beneficial ownership mapping is hardest and regulatory tolerance for errors is lowest.

Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

You can find more information:

NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography 

G7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sector 

CMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

title: Emirates NBD and BlackRock Launch Two Funds at Partnership Anniversary
snippet: The one-year-old collaboration has gathered $350m in AUM and now expands into CLO and systematic income strategies for retail wealth clients. The post Emirates NBD and BlackRock Launch Two Funds at Partnership Anniversary appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Emirates NBD Asset Management and BlackRock have launched two income-focused public funds to mark the first anniversary of their strategic partnership, broadening a collaboration that began in 2025 with access to private market alternatives and has since accumulated $350 million in assets under management.

The two new products are the FundStar Emirates CLO AA Fund, sub-managed by BlackRock, and the Emirates Systematic Income and Growth Fund, for which BlackRock serves as investment adviser while Emirates NBD Asset Management retains portfolio management responsibility. Both are now available to the bank’s retail and wealth clients across the region.

The funds in detail

The CLO fund invests in a portfolio of senior secured corporate loans across the US and Europe, targeting an average credit rating of AA with no sub-investment-grade exposure. It offers daily liquidity and carries no leverage, positioning it as a relatively conservative floating-rate income vehicle. BlackRock’s CLO franchise spans more than 24 years and manages over $40 billion globally in the strategy, which lends the product credible institutional provenance.

The Systematic Income and Growth Fund takes a benchmark-unconstrained approach, allocating across globally diversified income-producing assets using BlackRock’s systematic investment models. It targets a net distribution rate of 7% per annum, paid quarterly. That headline yield will attract scrutiny from wealth advisers assessing whether the return compensates adequately for the underlying complexity and variability of a multi-asset systematic strategy.

Michail Samawi, senior executive officer at Emirates NBD Asset Management, described the launch as fulfilling a commitment to “democratise premium global investments” for Middle East wealth clients. Keith Saldanha, BlackRock’s head of wealth and global product solutions for the Middle East and Africa, said the partnership demonstrated “significant opportunity for both CLO and systematic strategies within wealth portfolios.”

Market context and regulatory read-across

The move from private-market-only structures aimed at professional clients to public funds accessible to retail investors is a material step. Retail-eligible fund structures in the UAE fall under the oversight of the Securities and Commodities Authority, which has tightened disclosure and suitability requirements for complex products in recent years. The transition signals Emirates NBD Asset Management’s confidence that its distribution infrastructure and compliance framework can support a broader investor base, but it also raises the bar for product documentation and ongoing suitability assessment.

The CLO market itself has attracted renewed institutional interest across the Gulf, as dollar-denominated floating-rate products offer a natural hedge against rate uncertainty that regional investors with dollar-pegged liabilities value. Several global asset managers, including but not limited to BlackRock, have sought to package CLO exposure into fund wrappers accessible below institutional minimums, responding to strong private banking demand in Dubai and Riyadh.

The partnership model here, where a regional bank provides distribution and local regulatory relationships while a global manager provides investment capability, is becoming a standard template across the Gulf Cooperation Council. Similar structures have emerged between regional banks and global alternatives managers in Saudi Arabia under the Capital Market Authority‘s push to deepen local capital markets. The competitive question for Emirates NBD Asset Management is how quickly it can grow AUM in the new public funds relative to the $350 million gathered in the first year, and whether the 7% distribution target on the systematic fund holds across a full market cycle.

title: Boost Payment Solutions Partners Airwallex for Cross-Border B2B Cards
snippet: Boost says payment volume processed through Airwallex grew nearly ten-fold in five months, with 270 international supplier accounts onboarded. The post Boost Payment Solutions Partners Airwallex for Cross-Border B2B Cards appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Boost Payment Solutions has formalised a commercial partnership with Airwallex, under which the Melbourne-founded fintech provides global processing and acquiring infrastructure for Boost’s B2B card payments business. The arrangement has been running for five months and, according to both companies, has already delivered a near ten-fold increase in payment volume processed through the Airwallex rails, alongside the onboarding of more than 270 international supplier accounts.

Dean M. Leavitt, founder and CEO at Boost Payment Solutions

The partnership targets a structural pain point in cross-border B2B card acceptance. When a buying enterprise wants to pay an international supplier by commercial card, the friction typically lands on the supplier side: slow onboarding, elevated failure rates, retry loops that delay settlement, and processing costs that make wire transfer look more attractive. Boost says the integration addresses each of those: suppliers can go live in as few as two business days, payment failure rates are lower, and eligible high-value transactions are routed to qualify for large-ticket interchange rates. European flows are also said to benefit from optimised scheme fees.

Dean M. Leavitt, founder and chief executive of Boost Payment Solutions, said the partnership was about infrastructure consistency at scale. “Global B2B payments shouldn’t become more complicated simply because a business crosses a border,” he said. “By combining their global processing capabilities with our specialised B2B expertise, we can continue raising the bar for the customers and suppliers we serve.”

The commercial logic

The division of labour is legible. Airwallex holds more than 85 licences across North and Latin America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific, giving it a regulated acquiring footprint that would take years and significant capital to replicate independently. Boost, founded in New York in 2009 and active in more than 180 countries, brings proprietary technology for large-ticket card optimisation and the supplier-side commercial relationships that acquiring infrastructure alone cannot provide. Neither company disclosed revenue figures, processing volumes in absolute terms, or the commercial structure of the arrangement.

The “nearly ten-fold” volume growth figure is notable but should be read in context. A ten-fold increase from a low base can be achieved quickly during an active onboarding push; the more durable signal will be retention rates among those 270-plus suppliers and whether average transaction values justify the large-ticket interchange positioning.

Market context and regulatory read-across

The B2B cross-border card market is undergoing sustained structural change. Historically dominated by wire transfers and paper cheque, it has been shifting toward card-based and virtual card programmes as buyers seek the working-capital float, rebate income and data enrichment that cards provide. Several infrastructure providers, including Convera, Nuvei and Flywire among others, compete for the large-ticket B2B acquiring segment, while banking-as-a-service layers increasingly enter from below.

Regulatory tailwinds and headwinds are both in play. The European interchange caps introduced under the Interchange Fee Regulation have compressed margin on consumer card flows, making B2B and commercial card corridors proportionally more attractive to acquirers. At the same time, PSD3 and the forthcoming Payment Services Regulation in the EU are expected to sharpen rules around cross-border payment transparency and failure-rate disclosure, which could raise the bar for the kind of performance claims Boost and Airwallex are making in this release.

Airwallex’s licence count and dual headquarters in San Francisco and Singapore reflect a deliberate strategy to be domestically regulated in major corridors rather than relying on passporting. That approach becomes more commercially durable as regulators worldwide move away from light-touch treatment of non-bank payment firms. For Boost, the partnership is a way to inherit that regulatory infrastructure without bearing the full compliance overhead internally. The next milestone to watch is whether the partnership is extended to additional acquiring markets or whether Boost eventually seeks its own acquiring licences in key corridors.

Dive Brief:

First Citizens Bank is partnering with NCR Atleos to offer surcharge-free access to services via ATMs located at some 2,000 Target stores, the bank said in a press release last month. As part of the agreement, the bank’s customers can use the ATMs at Target stores to withdraw cash, check their account balances and transfer funds to eligible linked accounts without paying a fee, according to the Oct. 19 release.

“The consumer banking experience needs to meet customers where they are through multiple channels, whether in-person or digitally enabled,” First Citizens Bank’s head of consumer banking, Michael Wilson, said in the release. 

Meanwhile, NCR Atleos CEO Tim Oliver said Wednesday that the company’s sale to Brink’s is progressing, with expected completion of the transaction by January.

Dive Insight:

For NCR Atleos, which became a standalone company three years ago, the partnership with First Citizens allows it to add new service providers to its roster. 

The company separated from its parent in late 2023, creating two publicly traded companies: NCR Voyix and NCR Atleos. While NCR Atleos offers ATMs and other interactive teller machines for payments and banking services, NCR Voyix offers point-of-sale hardware and related services to restaurant, retail and other merchants.

As NCR Atleos has grown its corporate clientele, including by working with American Express and PayNearMe in recent years, its self-service banking segment has bolstered revenue. The company reported third-quarter earnings results Wednesday that showed its self-service banking segment rose 3% to $2.17 billion for the first nine months of the year, faster than its overall business revenue growth, which increased 2% to $3.23 billion for the period, according to the earnings press release. 

“Our service-led growth initiatives and investment in product innovation are encouraging financial institutions and retailers to choose our differentiated and comprehensive offering to meet their evolving self-service needs,” Oliver said in August when the company reported second-quarter earnings. 

NCR’s partnership with First Citizens comes as the ATM provider prepares to be acquired. In February, the Brink’s Company agreed to buy NCR Atleos in a cash and stock transaction valued at about $6.6 billion. As part of the deal, Brink’s will also take on $2.6 billion in NCR Atleos debt, a press release on the transaction said. 

Regulators have yet to approve the deal. The Competition and Markets Authority in the U.K. said Brink’s acquisition of NCR Atleos could limit competition, according to a September report from the news outlet Reuters. Earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal reported Brink’s plans to sell some subsidiaries in a move aimed at assuaging U.K. concerns.

“We continue to make meaningful progress on regulatory approval processes across the multiple jurisdictions, and have significantly advanced the integration planning activities for the pending combination of Atleos and The Brink’s Company,” Oliver said in the release this week.

title: FIS, Toast CFOs exit
snippet: The chief financial officers are leaving the payments players as the companies grapple with separate challenges.
fullText:
Fidelity National Information Services and Toast separately disclosed that their chief financial officers are exiting, as they also announced third-quarter earnings results. 

At FIS, which provides payments services to banking and capital markets clients, the company announced the departure of James Kehoe, with no further explanation. Alexandra “Alex” Brooks will step into the CFO post on an interim basis starting Thursday as the company begins a search for a permanent replacement, according to a Wednesday press release.

The CFO change at Jacksonville, Florida-based FIS landed as the company adjusted its financial forecasts due to unexpected changes in the outlook for recurring revenue, citing new factors that are dragging on that income.

The shifts were mainly related to changed expectations at some of its banking clients as those customers encounter implementation delays and, in some cases, work through acquisition activity, CEO Stephanie Ferris explained on a webcast with analysts Wednesday. The change is happening as some customers move from services with more traditional licenses to the company’s more updated subscription software services, she said.

“Over the course of the third quarter, we started to see some client-directed conversion delays, primarily in our larger client base, and some impacts from the timing around large bank consolidation,” Ferris said on the webcast.

FIS divests prepaid business

She also noted that the company would invest in technology and security to assist clients with implementations and to prioritize cyber work.

“These factors will weigh on our results in the fourth quarter in 2027, and we expect them to largely fade in 2028,” Ferris said. 

FIS also disclosed during the third-quarter report that it had sold what it referred to as a “non-core, prepaid asset” for $100 million. A spokesperson for the company didn’t immediately respond to requests for more information about the unit or the buyer.

Kehoe has been with FIS since August 2023, joining shortly after Ferris became CEO in January of that year. Together, they took the company through a $24.25 billion sale last year of its merchants services business Worldpay to Global Payments, and the $13.5 billion acquisition of a card issuer business from Global Payments.

FIS reported third-quarter adjusted net earnings rose 5.3% to $831 million as operating revenue climbed 29%, on an adjusted basis, to $3.37 billion, according to the company’s earnings press release.

At Toast, the digital payments processor said that its president and chief financial officer, Elena Gomez, will leave her posts at the end of the year. Michael Senno, who has served as Toast’s senior vice president of finance, will become CFO at that time, the company said.

Gomez, who has been at Toast since May 2021 and guided the company through its initial public offering that year, said in the company’s earnings press release that it’s time “to take a break before my next chapter.”

Toast CEO criticizes lawsuit

Meanwhile, during a webcast with analysts on Tuesday, Toast’s CEO, Aman Narang, continued to make a case for fighting a lawsuit brought by the Federal Trade Commission and states last week. The federal and state regulators alleged in their lawsuit that the company exacted “hidden fees” and “unauthorized charges” from both merchants and consumers. 

Narang defended the contracts Toast negotiates with every restaurant, and other merchants, to provide services in the business-to-business industry. 

The lawsuit turns on the Federal Trade Commission Act and the Restore Online Shoppers’ Confidence Act, barring companies from misleading customers. The regulators said Toast made “false or misleading claims” regarding its subscription and financing services; failed to make required disclosures; didn’t provide simple ways for customers to cancel their subscription; and charged customers without their consent. 

“We are incredibly disappointed with the FTC's decision to file the suit,” Narang told analysts on the earnings webcast. “We've been engaged with them and cooperating with them really over the past year, and fundamentally believe their application of ROSCA is unprecedented for custom contracts in B2B.”

Narang posited that the enforcement action on that basis could impact the entire industry. “If ROSCA were to apply to B2B custom negotiated contracts in a B2B context, it would have huge implications for, really, the whole industry and business contracts in general,” Narang contended. “We have a lot of confidence in our business practices and are ready to defend ourselves.” 

Toast reported third-quarter net income rose 60% to $169 million as revenue increased 21% to $1.98 billion, according to the earnings press release.

The CFOs at both FIS and Toast said they’ll continue to work with the companies to transfer their duties to their successors.

Riverside Payments and its affiliates agreed to pay $600,000 to resolve allegations they misled small businesses about processing costs.

        

            

        Published Nov. 4, 2026

First published on

    

    

                    

Dive Brief:

Payment processor Riverside Payments, its affiliate Cascade Equipment Leasing LLC and their operators have agreed to pay $600,000 to settle allegations that they deceived small businesses about payment-processing costs and cancellation terms, the Federal Trade Commission said Monday.

The proposed settlement, which stems from a joint action with Washington state, also allows affected small businesses to terminate their payment-processing agreements without an early termination penalty, the FTC said.

“Riverside and Cascade promised small businesses significant savings, but instead of saving money locked them into costly, multi-year contracts and made it very difficult to cancel,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a press release. “The FTC will hold accountable companies that deceive small businesses, whose hard work powers our economy.”

Dive Insight:

The FTC and Washington alleged in their complaint that Riverside promised businesses they could save 40% to 60% by switching payment processors. In reality, businesses that switched typically ended up paying more than they had with their previous providers, according to the complaint, which was filed Monday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington, along with a proposed order resolving the charges.

The companies allegedly failed to disclose several fees in sales quotes, including activation fees, batch fees and charges related to data security compliance or inactive processing, the government alleged. Riverside also allegedly buried important contract terms in a 26-page electronic agreement.

Those terms included automatic renewal of payment-processing services after an initial three-year contract, a $695 early termination fee and equipment leases through Cascade that extended one year beyond the processing agreement, according to the complaint.

The FTC and Washington also allege Riverside advertised a “no-risk” cancellation guarantee, promising customers they could cancel at any time without penalty, switch back to their previous processor and receive $500 for their time and trouble. Businesses seeking to leave instead allegedly faced repeated phone calls and delays, with some never receiving promised callbacks.

The complaint also challenges Riverside's earnings claims to prospective sales agents. The company advertised that agents could earn $75,000 to $95,000 annually, with top performers making $100,000. In reality, agents earned an average of $3,787 per year, according to the complaint.

The proposed order imposes a $32.1 million judgment against Riverside, Cascade and their owners, Brandon Skinner and Jason Reese. The judgment will be suspended after the defendants pay $600,000 because of their alleged inability to pay the full amount, the FTC said. The full judgment would be due if they are found to have misrepresented their financial circumstances, the agency said in its press release.

The order also requires the defendants to notify customers that they can terminate their merchant-processing agreements without paying early termination fees or other penalties during a 60-day period.

Under the proposed order, the companies would be prohibited from misrepresenting service costs, potential savings and cancellation terms. They would also have to disclose material contract terms before collecting billing information, obtain customers' express informed consent for recurring billing arrangements and provide a straightforward cancellation process.

The companies could not be reached for comment.

fullText:
Speech by Nikhil Rathi, FCA chief executive at the Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner, Mansion House.

  

Speaker: Nikhil Rathi, chief executive 

Event: Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner 

Delivered: 22 October 2026 

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Highlights

The UK’s financial services strength provides a platform to lead the next era of technology-driven growth. 

We must move faster and focus on outcomes to protect market integrity without holding back innovation. 

The FCA will make better use of technology and intelligence and more assertive use of its powers to tackle system-wide risks and financial crime. 

Stronger partnerships between regulators, industry, government and others is essential to protect market integrity.

    

            						

The success of the UK’s financial services

In August, flight cancellations left my sons and I with an extra day in Boston.   

A Red Sox game, perhaps? No, the Rathi boys – naturally – headed straight to…the Museum of American Finance.

Funded by industry, the museum celebrates the role of finance in American life. Illuminating the powerful benefits of informed risk taking.

Three sceptical boys engrossed for nearly 2 hours. I quite enjoyed it too.

It struck me though how right George Bernard Shaw was: Britain and America are 2 countries separated by a common language.

On this side of the pond, we’re perhaps more reserved, embarrassed even, talking about why finance matters. Yet there’s plenty to cheer.

We are the world’s biggest cross-border banking, foreign exchange (FX) and derivatives trading centre. We’re second in investment management … And our commercial insurance sector has doubled in size over a decade…

A financial services sector built on trust and one the whole United Kingdom should be proud of…  

Even more so as new technologies, so many owing to our research base, transform our economy and society.

UK firms leading in:

artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and tokenisation.

consumer access to investment opportunities widened.

moving from Open Banking to Open Finance.

Lady Mayor, your myth busting campaigns have championed London and the City. Thank you for your leadership.

If we can capture this opportunity, we gain in productivity… With rewards of economic growth felt across the country.

          

            						

I say 'we' because the FCA plays an important role.

Financial services businesses and investors need confidence in markets…including their ability to withstand and recover from shocks.

That’s why ensuring the integrity of the financial services system is an FCA primary objective.

Tonight, I want to explain how we maintain it as technology accelerates exponentially. Because, while we may be getting past peak rule making, we are nowhere near peak reform or innovation. Nor past the peak intervention required to disrupt harm and support market integrity and growth.

We have seen radical technological change before… But never so widespread or disruptive. Nor combined, as now, with a new geopolitical and defence order.

The trouble is our system responds too slowly. And trust in institutions is eroded if we can’t solve problems quickly.

Regulation takes time. Legislation requires scrutiny. Parliamentary resource is precious.

Our judicial system is under immense pressure, with more litigation and weightier decisions. We risk delays becoming the norm, with legal claims written with AI’s help potentially making things worse.

We all play a part in a system that prioritises safety in process over ruthless focus on outcomes and delivery.

So, the UK finds itself in a dangerous 'innovation delta': where institutions tasked with regulating markets and the mechanisms holding us accountable lag behind.

If we maintain an analogue approach in a digital age, new products enter the market faster than we adapt… Leaving us reacting to, even overwhelmed by, changes rather than shaping conditions for the UK to thrive.

Take Meta Muse, launched 6 weeks ago, one of the fastest-downloaded apps in US history. Personal agents are profoundly changing how consumers interact with financial and health services. Such applications will reach UK consumers soon.

Frontier AI models are here, making it easier for AI agents to carry out tasks increasingly autonomously. You are fast adopters.

And rapid change in wholesale markets:

decentralised finance

24/7 trading a reality with prices increasingly forming over weekends

parallel market structures operating alongside traditional ones

Vast opportunities. But the threats to market integrity are as serious as I have seen them.

Unprecedented volatility, concentration risks, new forms of market abuse and rampant cross-border financial crime: fast-emerging technologies putting these on steroids.

Cyber security too mixes the frailties of human nature and high tech.

Our own AI minister recently said it was likely that at some point the UK’s systems will be breached. Which is why reporting and learning from near misses is so important. As is insurance for you, your customers and supply chain.

Prevention will not always work, so investment in recovery is a necessity. The gravity of the decision to press a kill switch may pale in significance with the enormity of the task to get a system running again.

In the face of all today’s challenges, the temptation is to say: 'write more rules, but do it damned well faster'.

We will, where we need to… Including aligning with any national or global AI standards, which the Prime Minister has said will be a focus of the UK’s upcoming G20 presidency.

But if policymaking is our only regulatory reflex, we’ll be stuck chasing yesterday’s market instead of embracing the one in front of us.

          

            						

Regulatory reform continues

I do not mean to suggest that we will slow down rule reform or modernisation. But our focus must be on outcomes.

We have reformed our rulebook and strengthened our operations. Capital market reforms have kicked in. 

Technology is making it easier to interact with us with reduced reporting burdens. Our widest ever range of innovation services with record demand.

And we promised less intensive supervision for those clearly trying to do the right thing, so we can focus where harm is greatest.

But the impact won’t be fully felt unless we also end tickbox compliance. Reams of potentially duplicative assurance – data packs, risk reports, internal audit. Some of these processes driven by commercial choice, others by regulation and legislation.

Sarah Pritchard, the FCA’s deputy chief executive, will engage with you to streamline unnecessary effort…. To give Boards confidence to be brave. And consider if it’s time to look again at the 3 lines of defence.

As much as 8% of banks’ workforces are dedicated to combatting crime. We should be delivering far better outcomes with those resources.

Yet we’re bogged down by excessive data collection, complex validation, and a limited ability to understand a customer’s wider context and identify risks that span borders, institutions and accounts…

As we integrate over 60,000 professional services businesses into our ambit, Johan Sekora, our new chief operating officer, who previously led Swedish banks' intelligence sharing efforts, will spearhead work to look beyond know your customer (KYC) process so we unearth actual money laundering.

Information collected through KYC, transaction and sanctions monitoring will remain valuable.

We are ready to experiment, so we can focus collective resources exactly where they are needed….

Within the FCA, too, we must continue to get better at joining up the dots. AI tools give our supervisors a richer risk picture…

…Agents can assess cases, synthesise returns and intelligence… parse millions of rows of data and identify missing or concerning information…

Freeing up our people to do the work we need experts to do: to make the hardest decisions… Such as when agentic coordination becomes market manipulation. Or judging when a risk becomes system-wide.

Expanded capability means we’ll find more risks. So, we’ll need to be open about which justify the use of resources and which don’t.

          

            						

Powers and partnership

As an institution, we have not always persuaded others of the need for legislative change… And even when we have, change has been welcome but often slow.

So: how can we do our job effectively when technology advances faster than we can write laws or rules?

The answer must be to rethink how we use powers we already have.

We have system-wide responsibilities, but a fixed view of who we explicitly regulate.

Government and Parliament decide who we authorise. This perimeter is our anchor. But we cannot let it weigh so heavily that it sinks the regulatory ship.

Today’s risks aren’t polite enough to knock on our door to introduce themselves.

Market, cyber, or criminal risks emerge from multiple networks, firms and jurisdictions….

Capital flows across sectors, regulated or not, creating complex webs of commercial incentives. And harms within our remit originating outside it. Be that mass digital harm on social media.

Insider trading on offshore gambling or prediction markets. Or outages – like Google Cloud this week – disrupting people’s access to vital services. Talk of such system-wide risks is far from academic.

Money laundering through the regulated system is not just about fraud, sanctions and tax evasion, it funds human and drugs trafficking. Their victims: society’s most vulnerable.

Parliament has provided tools to deal with such system-wide issues affecting our objectives and remit:

The Enterprise, Consumer Rights and Online Safety and Digital Market Acts to name 4.

The critical third-parties regime. An expanding anti-money-laundering remit.

It isn’t enough to ask: is this in our perimeter?

If significant harm affects markets within our remit, we should ask: what powers do we have to tackle it? Would this be a good use of resources?

The same is true of growth opportunities. Not what are they, but how can we enable them?

In every instance: who can we work with to make a difference, quickly? Because no single agency can rise to today’s challenges alone.

Working with the Met, National Crime Agency and HMRC, we’ve recently undertaken 2 of our most significant operations to disrupt suspected organised criminal gangs who seek to abuse our financial system.

So, effective partnerships are already in action:

Cooperation through the Digital Regulators Forum on Meta Muse.

A big delivery year for pensions with the Pensions Regulator and DWP.

A FCA-Bank of England roadmap on digital assets soon dovetailing with the work Chris Woolard and the industry have been doing.

And work with international counterparts.

Recent action by US authorities against anti-money laundering violations confirming the fight against financial crime remains global. 

          

            						

Call to action: we need you

We should also be open to ideas about how we can act at pace and scale.

We have seen dedicated financial services courts speed things up in other markets, for example… And the accountability system could foster collaborative working.

There are significant mechanisms to hold the FCA accountable, more than for most regulators. Appropriate given the significance of our work and the breadth of powers entrusted to us.

But accountability must be system-wide too. Whether that is to press hard on growth or engage on risks, and which are priorities and which aren’t.

Parliament is the only body that can ensure accountability across rather than within narrow remits, transcending traditional committee boundaries.

And as we significantly step up the intensity of our activity to address system-wide risks, we need you.

The earlier we can work with you – the firms we regulate and civil society – to identify emerging risks and opportunities, the faster we can give you the confidence to move.

          

            						

Close: the prize

In other words, partnership.

That is what we need now. Partnership not just between financial regulators but more widely.

title: Debenhams Group Embeds Storfund Daily Advance for 30,000 Sellers
snippet: Debenhams Group has partnered with Storfund to give marketplace sellers up to 80% of shipped-order revenue daily, ahead of peak Christmas trading. The post Debenhams Group Embeds Storfund Daily Advance for 30,000 Sellers appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Debenhams Group has embedded Storfund‘s Daily Advance product directly into its marketplace platform, giving more than 30,000 brand partners access to up to 80% of their shipped-order revenue on a daily basis rather than waiting for the standard settlement cycle. The service went live in October 2026, timed ahead of the Christmas peak trading window.

Dan Finley, Group CEO at Debenhams Group

Under the arrangement, Storfund advances the 80% share each day as orders are dispatched. When Debenhams Group makes its scheduled marketplace payment to a partner, the funds flow into a Storfund-nominated account, at which point Storfund releases the remaining 20% to the seller, net of applicable fees. Participation is optional, subject to Storfund eligibility criteria, and carries no subscription, set-up fee or minimum term. Eligible sellers can use the service across Debenhams, boohoo and PrettyLittleThing without additional administration.

Dan Finley, chief executive of Debenhams Group, said the move was designed to make Debenhams Group the preferred platform for brands seeking to scale: “Giving sellers faster access to their sales revenue gives them greater flexibility to reinvest in their businesses when they need it most, particularly as we head into peak Christmas trading.”

The marketplace liquidity play

The launch is a structural extension of Debenhams Group’s broader pivot towards a marketplace model. Marketplace now accounts for 38.9% of the group’s gross merchandise value, up from 32.7% in the comparable period a year earlier, a shift that positions the group closer to a platform operator than a traditional retailer. Faster seller liquidity is a lever that platform operators use to attract and retain supply: when sellers can recycle working capital quickly, they hold deeper stock, respond faster to demand signals and are less likely to de-prioritise a platform in favour of a competitor with quicker settlement.

Storfund positions itself as a liquidity layer for marketplace sellers globally, with existing integrations on Amazon, TikTok Shop and Booking.com. Justin Hanna, the company’s director of platform partnerships, framed the Debenhams integration as part of a broader market trajectory: “Marketplaces have spent the last decade building better shopping, advertising, fulfilment and settlement experiences. Liquidity is the next frontier.”

Market context and competitive read-across

Marketplace seller financing is an increasingly contested segment. Amazon operates its own Lending programme for third-party sellers, while several specialist working-capital providers, including Payoneer, Clearco and Uncapped, compete for the same cohort of e-commerce businesses. The distinguishing feature of an embedded model, where the advance product sits inside the marketplace rather than requiring a seller to seek out a standalone lender, is friction reduction: eligibility can be tied to platform data rather than traditional credit underwriting.

From a regulatory standpoint, the product as described resembles a revenue-based advance or purchase-of-receivables arrangement rather than a consumer credit facility, which typically places it outside the FCA‘s consumer credit regime. However, if Storfund’s eligibility and fee structures are applied to smaller sole-trader sellers, the regulatory perimeter warrants monitoring as the FCA continues to refine its approach to buy-now-pay-later and alternative credit instruments.

The forward indicators to watch are the take-up rate among Debenhams Group’s seller base, whether Storfund extends the integration to the full set of group marketplaces beyond the three named at launch, and any update on fee economics that would allow an independent assessment of the cost of capital for sellers using the service.

title: Cards draw customers, Marqeta CEO says
snippet: Companies have found there’s “almost nothing more engaging than a card,” CEO Mike Milotich said this week in an interview.
fullText:
Marqeta is attracting business from large companies that want to issue payment cards and other embedded services to deepen engagement with their customers, the fintech’s chief executive said in an interview this week.

Fortune 500 enterprises have recognized the power of card products due to the success and growth of fintechs’ services, CEO Mike Milotich said Wednesday in an interview, a day after the company reported third-quarter financial results and raised its profit outlook for 2026.

From the leader of a company that issues virtual and physical payments cards, his perspective is to be expected.

“People are realizing … that there’s almost nothing more engaging than a card product,” Milotich said. “A lot of these businesses are looking for engagement, they’re looking to drive their core business through a card product, getting you in their app, using their system, (and) their platform more.”

That trend directly benefits Marqeta, an Oakland, California-based fintech that also provides embedded finance services, including payment processing.

The average consumer uses a payment card 2.5 times each day, Milotich said, without providing details. “Besides maybe younger people checking their Instagram or something, there are very few things that people do that frequently,” he quipped.

A large company already has a significant customer base, which makes it easier “to insert a financial product” into its existing platforms, he said.

Marqeta enjoys “a long runway for growth” as the company “has barely scratched the surface (<1%) in a large addressable market of card-based money movement” totaling about $30 trillion, KBW analysts wrote Tuesday in a client note. 

However, the company sits at a point where growth from its top clients, including buy now, pay later companies, could decelerate and “new wins could take time to ramp,” they added.

Milotich, Marqeta’s former chief financial officer, was appointed to the top post on an interim basis in February 2025 and became CEO seven months later. The company has about 950 employees, a spokesperson said.

Marqeta’s larger customers also like the ability to have embedded solutions bundled, letting them avoid piecing together multiple vendors for each part of their planned offering, said Milotich, a former Visa executive who has also worked at PayPal Holdings and American Express.

“We can go to any customer and say, ‘If you want to do stablecoin, we have three options for you. We’ve already done the work and integrated, you can pull it through our APIs,’” he said. “That’s sort of where the business is moving.”

Last month, for example, Marqeta and the cryptocurrency platform Coinbase partnered on a stablecoin-backed payment card, allowing Marqeta customers to offer cards that apply stablecoin balances at merchants that accept cards.

The company has also announced a recent partnership with Google, for digital wallet tools aimed at children and parents. Last month, it worked with Square’s parent, Block, to introduce a business credit card for Square sellers – Marqeta’s first product on the American Express card network – as Block consolidated its Square cards.

For the third quarter, Marqeta reported net income of $115.4 million, compared to a $3.6 million loss in the same period last year, with total processing volume rising 29% to $126.5 billion. Revenue was $176.2 million, an 8% gain from the same quarter of 2025.

Block – the parent of Cash App, Square and Afterpay – accounted for 41% of Marqeta revenue in the quarter, down from 45% for the full year last year, according to regulatory filings, as that company has diversified its suppliers. Other Marqeta customers include Affirm Holdings, DoorDash, Uber Technologies and Western Union.

title: Fundcraft and Stella Partner to Open Private Markets to Wealth Channel
snippet: The two firms aim to build a repeatable cross-border model for private markets fund launches, with the first vehicle targeted for January 2027. The post Fundcraft and Stella Partner to Open Private Markets to Wealth Channel appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
fundcraft, the Luxembourg and France-regulated digital fund operations provider, has agreed a partnership with Stella, a Paris-based private markets distribution specialist founded in April 2026. The collaboration is designed to help alternative asset managers launch and scale private markets strategies through the wealth management channel across France and wider Europe, with a first fund targeted for launch in January 2027.

The partnership links fundcraft’s regulated infrastructure, it holds a CSSF licence as an AIFM and central administrator in Luxembourg and operates an AMF-authorised portfolio management company in France, with Stella’s network of approximately 500 wealth advisers, private banks and family offices, including CGPs, independent financial advisers and single and multi-family offices. Stella’s platform is being connected to fundcraft’s fund operations infrastructure ahead of the first launch.

The operational problem being solved

Thomas Ibanez, country head,France at fundcraft

The strategic logic rests on a structural shift in private markets distribution. According to figures cited by BlackRock and referenced in the announcement, more than two-thirds of EMEA wealth investors currently allocate only 0–5% of their portfolios to private markets. Allocations from high-net-worth and affluent investors are projected to more than double by 2030, with over 70% of EMEA wealth investors expected to hold between 5% and 20% in the asset class by that point.

That growth trajectory creates a meaningful operational challenge. Institutional private markets strategies were built for a relatively small number of large investors, concentrated reporting relationships and a single domicile. Routing the same strategies through wealth channels means accommodating higher investor volumes, smaller ticket sizes, multiple distribution partners, unit-linked life insurance wrappers and differing regulatory requirements across markets. Each of those variables adds complexity to onboarding, subscriptions, transfer agency and reporting.

Thomas Ibanez, country head France at fundcraft, said: “More investors, more distribution relationships and more jurisdictions quickly multiply the operational complexity. Stella understands that channel and has built a strong network around it, while fundcraft provides the regulated and digital infrastructure behind the funds. By connecting the two, we can support managers with a model that is not only suitable for one launch, but can be reused as they bring new strategies and vehicles to market.”

The partnership is structured to avoid rebuilding the operating model for each new fund or market entry. Wealth-management partners already onboarded through Stella will be able to access successive fund launches through a consistent environment covering documentation, information and subscription workflows, while fundcraft handles regulated management, administration, investor operations and reporting.

Market context and regulatory read-across

The broader competitive landscape for private markets access infrastructure in Europe has grown significantly busier over the past two years. Several fund administration and fund-as-a-service providers compete for the ELTIF 2.0 and semi-liquid fund buildout, and distribution-technology firms are also targeting the CGP and family office segment in France and the Benelux. The ELTIF 2.0 framework, which came into force in January 2024, has materially lowered the minimum denomination threshold and expanded eligible assets, making the French and Luxembourg domiciles more attractive for retail-accessible alternatives. fundcraft already has live ELTIF 2.0 experience, having supported MIMCO’s Makers fund and the Openstone Infraworld evergreen infrastructure vehicle.

Stella is a newly formed firm, incorporated in April 2026, and its network of 500 wealth advisers represents relationships under development rather than a fully contracted distribution book. Managers evaluating the partnership will want to track conversion of that network into committed subscription capacity as the January 2027 first launch approaches. The structure of individual funds under the model, the specific managers involved and the ticket-size economics have not yet been disclosed.

fundcraft currently supports nearly 300 funds, representing more than 20,000 LP subscriptions and close to €20 billion in commitments and subscription targets, across clients including Moonfare, Stableton and Rocket Internet.

title: Shift4 signals caution
snippet: The payments processor is navigating weak demand for travel to Europe, and softer sales at its restaurant and hotel customers.
fullText:
Troubling economic conditions are continuing to vex Shift4 Payments, with the point-of-sale processor beset by travel weakness in Europe and reduced dining in the U.S.

Shift4 is navigating “a more challenging backdrop than we’ve seen in recent years,” CEO Taylor Lauber wrote in a shareholder letter accompanying the company’s third-quarter results on Thursday. The company cut its profit outlook and gross revenue target for the full year, with weak conditions expected to persist into 2027.

“Our business has been tested in many different ways this year, forcing us to adapt the business and make challenging calls,” Lauber said Thursday on a conference call with analysts to discuss the results. 

Fallout from the Iran conflict has bedeviled Shift4 in the European retail market, where it operates with Global Blue, the Swiss payments technology firm it acquired last year for $2.5 billion, including taking on $1 billion in debt. The Middle East and southeast Asia are significant sources of travel customers for Global Blue’s tax-free shopping business, which represents about 20% of Shift4 revenues. 

Beyond the European retail woes, inflation-fatigued Americans are also dining out less. Restaurant sales not only haven’t improved in the second half of 2026, as the company had expected, some comparisons turned negative in October relative to last year, Chief Financial Officer Christopher Cruz said.

Given the conditions, Shift4 has adopted “a conservatism in the way we're looking at the variety of challenges this year” for its financial modeling, as the overall operating environment makes it “hard not to be influenced towards a more cautious approach,” Cruz said in response to an analyst’s question about factors affecting Shift4’s views of 2027.

Shift4 also announced its purchase of Paramount Commerce, a Toronto-based pay-by-bank firm. Terms of the deal, expected to close in the next few weeks, were not disclosed. Paramount enables pay-by-bank deposits and payouts in Canada for companies that include the sports betting sites DraftKings and FanDuel, and Canadian telecommunications firm Telus, Shift4 said in its Thursday third-quarter earnings presentation.

“Bank rails carry the lion’s share of payment volumes in many markets, and account-to-account fits transactions where cards run into limits,” Lauber said on a conference call Thursday with analysts. “This is a kind of normal-course, tuck-in (purchase) that fits right into the Shift4 playbook.”

One issue troubling investors is that Shift4 has failed to articulate a long-term strategy, “especially around Global Blue,” William Blair analyst Andrew Jeffrey wrote last month in a report for the investment firm’s clients. 

The acquisition occurred under former CEO Jared Isaacman, who left the company last year when he was confirmed as administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

“Our sense is that investors still don’t have a good sense of why this deal happened, whether it was the former CEO’s passion project or it simply reflected a desire for scale,” Jeffrey wrote Oct. 20. Shift4 has “substantial cross-sell potential” with Global Blue among its smaller and medium sized business customers, but hasn’t yet demonstrated it can monetize a new POS device it rolled out to 15 European countries this year.

In a note Thursday, Jeffrey further suggested that Shift4 has relied on a dated model of buying independent software vendors and small acquirers at attractive prices, replacing legacy software systems, and monetizing the technology. 

“This strategy was successful when Shift4 was much smaller, money was free, the merchant processing industry was less competitive, and Shift4 had a knowledge advantage,” he wrote. “Those circumstances no longer exist, in our opinion.”

Shift4 shares have lost about 36% over the past year, including a 4.5% drop on Thursday.

“The share price has clearly not reflected the durability, diversity, and outright caliber of our business and the optimism we feel inside the company,” the CEO said, noting in his remarks that Shift4’s employees, management and founder own about 42% of the company, which is based near Allentown, Pennsylvania. 

Later in the call, Lauber said that “market sentiment in both our business and the broader sector is one that is not rewarding much and is punishing any misgivings.”
